title: Tilāñ juhomi: the sesame offering for good things
theme: Sesame offered into the fire with requests for a mind delighting in the divine, for the goods of a household, and for faith and understanding.

words.context: anon: «सरसान्न तु शुष्कान्» — moist, not dry
anon: «सपिष्टान्सक्त्वादिपिष्टान्तरलेशसहितान्» — with a little other meal such as barley-flour
anon: «गन्ध उत्तमदेहसौरभ्यमस्यास्तीति गन्धारस्तत्संबुद्धौ» — one who has fragrance; he takes it as the Supreme Self
anon: «त्वदीयाः परमपावना गुणा मम चित्ते रमन्तु» — may your most purifying qualities delight in my mind
anon: «गावो हिरण्यं धनमन्नपानमेतानि मम सिध्यन्तु» — may these be attained by me
anon: «श्रियै गजान्तलक्ष्मीसिद्ध्यर्थं» — for the attainment of wealth down to elephants

words.gram: f. acc. sg. (printed with short i)

words.context: anon: «आनृण्यतां देवर्षिपितॄणत्रयनिर्मुक्तत्वं» — freedom from the three debts to gods, sages and ancestors
anon: «ब्रह्मण्यं सर्वब्राह्मणोत्तमत्वं» — pre-eminence among brāhmaṇas (his gloss)
anon: «श्रद्धामेधे गुरुवेदान्तवाक्यविश्वासवेदशास्त्रार्थग्रहणधारणपटुत्वे» — trust in the teacher and the Vedānta, and skill in grasping and retaining the meaning of the Veda
anon: «भगवान्परमात्मा मह्मं सम्यग्ददातु» — may the Lord, the Supreme Self, grant me

sandhi.rule: tilān + juhomi → tilāñ juhomi: n becomes the palatal ñ before j.

sandhi.type: n before s and before g
sandhi.rule: sarasān + sapiṣṭān: the n is written as anusvāra before s; sapiṣṭān + gandhāra: the n stays before g.
dhanam + annapānam → dhanam annapānam, written together.
sarveṣām + śriyai → sarveṣāṃ śriyai, which the Taittirīya recitation writes सर्वेषाग् श्रियै.
ca + ānṛṇyatām → cānṛṇyatām, written with the doubled avagraha of the recitation text.

samasa.vigraha: बहवः पुत्राः यस्य सः बहुपुत्रः, तस्य भावः
samasa.meaning: the state of having many children

morphology.note: Accusative of lakṣmī, printed with a short i (लक्ष्मिं); the Tirupati e-text has लक्ष्मीं. The base and the Ānandāśrama text agree on the short vowel.
Abstract noun in -tā from the bahuvrīhi bahuputra, ‘having many children’.
Imperative 3rd singular of sam + √dā, written with its preverb; no subject is expressed. The commentator supplies ‘the Lord’.

translation.literal: I offer sesame seeds, moist, with meal; O fragrant one, may [they] delight in my mind. Svāhā. Cows, gold, wealth, food and drink, for the prosperity of all. Svāhā. Prosperity and fortune and nourishment and good name and freedom from debt, piety, having many children, faith and intelligence, offspring — may [he] grant. Svāhā.
translation.readable: I offer moist sesame seeds mixed with meal. O fragrant one, may [your qualities] dwell gladly in my mind. Svāhā. Cows, gold, wealth, food and drink — for the flourishing of all. Svāhā. May prosperity and fortune, nourishment and a good name, freedom from debt, piety, many children, faith and understanding, and offspring be granted. Svāhā.

syntax: Three offering formulas, each closed by svāhā. The first has a main verb in the first person (juhomi) with an object and two adjectives, then a vocative and a wish in the third-person imperative (ramantu) without an expressed subject. The second is a list of nominatives with a dative of purpose (śriyai) and no verb. The third is a long list of accusatives joined by ca, the object of the imperative sandadātu, again without an expressed subject.

ambiguities.note: ramantu has no subject in the text. The anonymous commentator supplies the qualities of the Supreme: «त्वदीयाः परमपावना गुणा मम चित्ते रमन्तु».
A vocative, ‘O fragrant one’, which the commentator takes as an address to the Supreme Self («हे गन्धार परमात्मंस्त्वदर्थं तिलाञ्जुहोमि»). The text does not say whom it addresses.
sandadātu has no subject here; in 10.64 the same list closes with jātavedaḥ sandadātu, addressing Agni Jātavedas. The commentator supplies the Lord.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Prose formulas with anuṣṭubh-like phrases. The five printed lines count 23, 18, 15, 8 and 12 syllables (svāhā included).

beginner: Here sesame seeds, moist and mixed with a little meal, are offered into the sacred fire with three short formulas, each ending with the call svāhā. The first asks that something divine take delight in the speaker’s mind. The second names the goods of a household — cows, gold, wealth, food and drink — and asks them for the flourishing of all. The third lists what a good life was thought to need: prosperity, a good name, freedom from debts, piety, children, faith and understanding. The old commentator says these mantras begin a fire ritual performed by someone about to renounce the world, to remove every fault first. The edition reports that use and makes no claim about what the offering brings.
analogy: Like a list made before a long journey: first the frame of mind, then the provisions, then what one hopes to carry inside.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Sesame is offered with a wish that [the god’s qualities] delight in the speaker’s mind; cows, gold, wealth, food and drink are named ‘for the prosperity of all’; and prosperity, fortune, nourishment, good name, freedom from debt, piety, many children, faith, intelligence and offspring are asked to be granted. Each formula ends with svāhā.

commentary.q: In what rite are these mantras used?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator says that from here on the mantras serve to remove all sin and belong to the virajā offering that forms part of taking up the fourth stage of life: «अतः परं सर्वपापनिबर्हणार्थाः सर्वोत्कृष्टचतुर्थाश्रमकरणाङ्गभूते». The one about to renounce performs them, «सर्वपापनिबर्हणद्वारा संन्यासं करिष्यमाणो», and the deity who receives every oblation is the Supreme Self: «सर्वत्र हविर्ग्राहिणी देवता तु परमात्मैव».

commentary.q: How does he read the requests?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He reads each item with a gloss: the sesame is moist and mixed with meal, «सरसान्न तु शुष्कान्सपिष्टान्सक्त्वादिपिष्टान्तरलेशसहितान्»; the prosperity is royal fortune and the ‘fortune’ is that of release, «श्रियं राज्यलक्ष्मीं» and «मोक्षलक्ष्मीं»; freedom from debt is freedom from the three debts, «आनृण्यतां देवर्षिपितॄणत्रयनिर्मुक्तत्वं»; faith and intelligence are trust in the teacher and skill in the Veda, «श्रद्धामेधे गुरुवेदान्तवाक्यविश्वासवेदशास्त्रार्थग्रहणधारणपटुत्वे». His gloss of brahmaṇyam as pre-eminence among brāhmaṇas is reported as his.

commentary.q: Where does the virajā series begin?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator makes these sesame mantras the start of the virajā offering. Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, on the Drāviḍa text, begins the virajā offerings later, with the series of purifications (our 10.65): «अथ सन्न्यासविषया विरजाहोमा एकपञ्चाशप्रभृतय एकादशानुवाकाः».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: the anonymous bhāṣya reads it as a ritual formula, and neither Sāyaṇa nor Bhāskara comments on it in the copies used (their 64-anuvāka texts do not include it). Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary is not in the sources. No school position is given.

contemporary.text: The three formulas move from the inner (a mind that delights in what is good) to the outer (goods shared ‘for the prosperity of all’) and back to the inner (faith and understanding). It is a compact picture of what a well-ordered life was thought to need. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you made a list of what a good life needs, which items from this one would you keep?
reflect.deeper: The commentator reads ‘fortune’ (lakṣmī) as the fortune of release, in a list of worldly goods. What does that reading do to the list?
reflect.practice: Name one thing you have that is ‘for the prosperity of all’, not only for yourself, and use it so today.

references.text: Only the anonymous bhāṣya comments on this anuvāka in the edition’s sources; Bhāskara is cited here only for where he begins the virajā series.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text lacks the final svāhā; the collation leaves it for review. It also reads लक्ष्मीं for लक्ष्मिं (a witness error by the collation’s rule).
The subjects of ramantu and sandadātu are not expressed; the commentator’s supplements are reported, not adopted.
